Issued at 224 PM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

This Afternoon through Tuesday Evening...

Low clouds, drizzle, and scattered light rain showers continue for 
many areas north of the KY Parkways at this hour, with satellite 
showing the back edge of the cool and drab weather lifting across 
south central KY. Where clearing has taken place, temperatures have 
quickly warmed into the low 70s. Between now and this evening, 
gradual clearing is expected as dry air advects in from the south 
and southeast. Where skies clear, a quick jump in temperatures from 
the upper 50s and low 60s to the upper 60s to near 70 would be 
expected. Drizzle and light rain should linger for a few more hours 
across northern and western portions of the CWA, though these areas 
should also clear by this evening.

Tonight, the clearing trend in low stratus should continue, though 
scattered to broken mid- and upper-level clouds are likely to remain 
into the day on Tuesday. A strengthening pressure gradient is 
expected overnight as low pressure over the Plains slowly moves 
toward the area. While a near-sfc stable layer should keep most of a 
40-kt LLJ aloft through the night, increasing southerly flow should 
keep temperatures mild, with lows in most locations only falling 
into the mid-to-upper 50s. Locations along and east of US 127 would 
have the best chance to fall into the low 50s Tuesday morning.

Tomorrow is expected to be an unseasonably warm and breezy day as a 
broad area of deep SW flow overspreads the Ohio Valley. As low-level 
lapse rates steepen with daytime heating, stronger winds aloft are 
expected to mix down to the surface. From mid-morning through the 
afternoon hours, expect southerly winds of 10 to 20 mph with wind 
gusts of 20 to 30 mph. If we can achieve an overlap of more 
sunshine/heating (better chances east of I-65) with stronger flow 
aloft (west of I-65), scattered gusts of 30 to 40 mph will be 
possible. Strong warm advection should send temperatures into the 
mid-to-upper 70s Tuesday afternoon, with a few spots potentially 
touching 80 degrees. While daily high temperature records appear 
safe at SDF (82) and BWG (82), LEX (78) would have the best chance 
of tying or setting a new record. Cloud cover will steadily increase 
from west to east through the afternoon and evening hours, with rain 
chances remaining 10 percent or less through the daytime hours.

Tuesday Night through Wednesday Night...

An amplified upper-level trough ejecting into the Plains this 
afternoon will become cutoff over the next 24 to 36 hours, slowly 
moving east toward the Upper Mississippi Valley by Wednesday 
morning. As the system becomes vertically stacked, its eastward 
progression is expected to slow, with a plume of strong IVT 
overspreading the Tennessee and Ohio Valley Tuesday night into 
Wednesday morning. Ensemble mean PW values are forecast to rise to 
1.6-1.8" ahead of the surface cold front, exceeding the 95th 
percentile of model climatology. Model soundings show deep 
saturation through much of the depth of the troposphere, promoting 
the development of precipitation late Tuesday night into the day on 
Wednesday.

The first few cycles of hi-res guidance which extend into Wednesday 
show a leading round of isolated to scattered showers around or just 
after midnight Wednesday, with the main line of showers and 
(potentially) embedded thunderstorms arriving a few hours before 
sunrise. Given the deep saturation, most model soundings show low 
amounts of instability, with ensemble MUCAPE values peaking around 
200-400 J/kg within the warm sector. It is also uncertain whether or 
not any surface-based instability will be realized, as soundings 
show fairly poor low-level lapse rates. With strong flow aloft 
expected, this lack of instability should keep the strong/severe 
storm potential to a minimum, and this thinking continues to be 
supported by AI/ML convective hazard guidance. Outside of the severe 
storm threat, the pressure gradient should continue to support 
breezy conditions through the day on Wednesday.

With the rich moisture in place, even a relatively narrow band of 
moderate to heavy showers will put down beneficial rainfall amounts. 
Most likely rainfall amounts range from 0.75" (southern IN) to 1.50" 
(southern KY) with this forecast issuance, with high end (10% 
exceedance probability) ranging from 2" in southern IN to 2.75" in 
southern KY. Even these high-end amounts are below 6-hr FFG, so 
nothing more than nuisance flooding is expected at this time. Rain 
should start to taper from west to east early Wednesday afternoon, 
with our eastern counties expected to clear by the late evening 
hours.
